title: Depressurizing the Body: The Bummer about Bedtime Revenge
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. names "bedtime revenge" (revenge bedtime procrastination) -- staying up late to reclaim a sense of autonomy after a day when work dictated everything -- and argues it is a losing trade, since the momentary sovereignty costs the body's capacity to actually be autonomous the next day. He lays out concrete sleep hygiene fundamentals (7+ hours, consistent sleep and wake times, a cool dark room, avoiding late meals or alcohol, daytime exercise) and frames them less as chores and more as an acknowledgment of human finitude. He shares his own history of "I'll sleep when I'm dead" macho overwork and how reading about sleep science changed his practice. The piece then turns practical, offering three power-nap variations teachers can use during a prep period and at-home strategies such as sleep hygiene audits and negotiating nap time with a partner. Throughout, rest is reframed as depressurization rather than laziness, situating sleep within the broader "life stewardship" discipline Stuart has been building across the blog.
points: Bedtime revenge feels like reclaiming autonomy but actually reduces it, because the sleep debt it creates diminishes the next day's capacity for genuine autonomy.

A short sleep-hygiene checklist -- consistent bedtime and wake time, a cool dark room, no late meals or alcohol, daytime exercise -- is offered as low-effort, high-leverage groundwork rather than an optional extra.

Three power-nap protocols (a plain 15-20 minute attempt, a no-pressure "just close your eyes" version, and the caffeine-primed "nappucino" drawn from Dan Pink's research) give teachers a concrete way to use prep periods for real recovery.
Reframing sleep as "depressurization" and as practicing the reality of being a finite creature turns a chore into a philosophical discipline, consistent with Stuart's broader stewardship framework.
quotes: But here's the problem (spoiler alert): bedtime revenge wins in the end. Because while we temporarily get that sweet moment of blissful sovereignty, it comes at the cost of waking up tomorrow with greater physical pressurization, which in turns diminishes our odds of experiencing autonomy in our normal waking hours.
It's us taking revenge on a day where we didn't experience much autonomy by stealing some free time from the stubbornly large number of hours that our bodies supposedly need to sleep.

Things started to change for me when I read a book about sleep and realized I was being a fool. So I started trying to get 7-8 hours per night, and it took me months before I started feeling the difference.

I used to dislike power naps because I felt so much pressure to fall asleep in the 15-20 minutes that I'd give myself for the nap. The pressure greatly reduced the restorative effects of the 15-20 minutes, and it often left me awake the whole time.
Dude. You don't have to fall asleep during a power nap. Just get comfortable and close your eyes for 15-20 minutes.
The most efficient nap is the nappucino. The caffeine won't fully engage in your bloodstream for about twenty-five minutes, so drink up right before you lie down.
Even as a kid, I often had to read a book in order to fall asleep. To make this less annoying to your spouse or partner, get them a sleep mask.
